comments.author: @mikahundin
comments.text:
Running AI models locally on-device instead of relying on cloud connectivity can provide significant benefits for user privacy and security. Here are some key advantages:

Privacy:
- Data never leaves the device, protecting sensitive personal information like voice recordings, messages, photos etc. from being transmitted over the internet and potentially intercepted or accessed by others.

- On-device processing prevents the need to upload personal data to company servers, where it could be collected, analyzed and monetized without user knowledge.

- User queries and interactions remain completely private to the individual device and are not sent externally where they could be logged or monitored.

Security:
- No data transfer means no potential for interception or "man-in-the-middle" attacks when communicating with remote servers over the internet.

- On-device AI eliminates the threat of server breaches exposing troves of user data stored in the cloud.

- Users are not dependent on an internet connection for core AI functionality, preventing downtimes or attacks that could disrupt cloud services.

- Processing happens within the trusted execution environment of the user's personal device versus opaque remote servers they have no control over.

By keeping personal data fully confined to the device, on-device AI basically eliminates privacy risks around data being collected, monetized or exposed by tech companies. It provides a secure, always-available experience completely under the user's control.

For a company like Apple that stresses privacy as a key value proposition, offering highly advanced on-device AI agents could be a powerful differentiator over rivals that rely more heavily on cloud-based AI processing user data externally.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
Tesla has been doing interesting things for their Full Self Driving project. Their work is not very transparent. But we do know some stuff about it.

We know that a couple years back, they eliminated around a thousand data labeling jobs. Data labelers were responsible for affixing text tags to video images, so FSD could start to figure out what it was seeing in live video feeds from a vehicle's cameras. Tesla no longer needed humans to do that. They invented autolabeling. AI does that now.

Tesla's hardware architecture from the start separated training compute from inference. Training compute is at data centers. Inference is in cars. They developed their own inference chips. Software, hardware and sensors together are imaginatively called Hardware plus a version number. Latest in-vehicle hardware is HW4. The inference engine works with or without an internet connection.

That's exactly the kind of split I expect to see from Apple and other developers.

Apple claims it will provide neural net inference chips for consumer devices. I have no idea how that will compare to Tesla's HW.

Labels provide context and help with accurately forecasting what detected objects might do.

LLM developers seem to be following in Tesla's footprints.

FSD is not an LLM (yet). It interprets sensor feeds, navigates, and drives the car. It's a single-mode model (video).

FSD Beta has now become FSD Supervised. It works very well (though it does make mistakes, still), so for now a human must be in the loop and paying attention.

I believe Google is close to releasing a phone with built-in inference for AI. I have no idea how much useful inference will come out of that.
